addedLines: - claude: Catch-all for any task that doesn't fit a more specific agent. FleetView's default when no agent name is typed. (Tools: *)

- claude-code-guide: Use this agent when the user asks questions ("Can Claude...", "Does Claude...", "How do I...") about: (1) Claude Code (the CLI tool) - features, hooks, slash commands, MCP servers, settings, IDE integrations, keyboard shortcuts; (2) Claude Agent SDK - building custom agents; (3) Claude API (formerly Anthropic API) - Messages API for directly passing messages to Claude, Tool Runner (`client.beta.messages.tool_runner`) for running an agentic loop over your own tools, manual tool-use loops, Managed Agents for server-hosted agents with a managed sandbox, prompt caching, and general Anthropic SDK usage; (4) Claude Tag (Claude in Slack) - what it is, setting it up for a Slack workspace, `/install-slack-app`; (5) `claude plugin eval` (writing and running plugin eval suites, its JSON/report, sandbox, CI, early-access enablement) and the `/skill-doctor` report. **IMPORTANT:** Before spawning a new agent, check if there is already a running or recently completed claude-code-guide agent that you can continue via SendMessage. (Tools: Bash, Read, WebFetch, WebSearch)
- dev: TDD Developer agent - implements features using test-driven development and clean code principles (Tools: All tools)

- entire-engineering:design:design-implementation-reviewer: Use this agent when you need to verify that a UI implementation matches its Figma design specifications. This agent should be called after code has been written to implement a design, particularly after HTML/CSS/React components have been created or modified. The agent will visually compare the live implementation against the Figma design and provide detailed feedback on discrepancies.

Examples:
- <example>
  Context: The user has just implemented a new component based on a Figma design.
  user: "I've finished implementing the hero section based on the Figma design"
  assistant: "I'll review how well your implementation matches the Figma design."
  <commentary>
  Since UI implementation has been completed, use the design-implementation-reviewer agent to compare the live version with Figma.
  </commentary>
  </example>
- <example>
  Context: After the general code agent has implemented design changes.
  user: "Update the button styles to match the new design system"
  assistant: "I've updated the button styles. Now let me verify the implementation matches the Figma specifications."
  <commentary>
  After implementing design changes, proactively use the design-implementation-reviewer to ensure accuracy.
  </commentary>
  </example> (Tools: All tools)

- entire-engineering:design:design-iterator: Use this agent PROACTIVELY when design work isn't coming together on the first attempt. If you've made 1-2 design changes and the result still feels off, suggest using this agent with 5x or 10x iterations for deeper refinement. This agent takes screenshots, analyzes what's not working, implements improvements, and repeats N times to systematically fix design issues. Perfect when colors feel wrong, layouts aren't balanced, or the overall aesthetic needs work that single changes can't achieve. <example>Context: User asks to change button color but result still looks off. user: "Change the button to blue" assistant: [makes change, takes screenshot] "The button is now blue, but I notice the overall color balance still feels off. Would you like me to use the design-iterator agent with 5 iterations to systematically improve the color harmony and visual balance?" <commentary>PROACTIVE USE: After a simple change doesn't fully resolve the design issue, suggest the design-iterator to do deeper work.</commentary></example> <example>Context: User's design request leads to something that doesn't look right. user: "Make the hero section more modern" assistant: [makes initial changes] "I've added some modern elements, but the result isn't quite coming together. This looks like it needs iterative refinement. Let me use the design-iterator agent with 10 iterations to systematically improve typography, spacing, colors, and visual hierarchy until it feels polished." <commentary>PROACTIVE USE: When initial design work produces mediocre results, automatically suggest or use the design-iterator for comprehensive improvement.</commentary></example> <example>Context: User wants explicit iterative refinement. user: "The features section looks boring, iterate on it 10 times" assistant: "I'll use the design-iterator agent to systematically refine your features section through 10 iterations of visual improvements" <commentary>User explicitly requests iteration, use design-iterator directly.</commentary></example> <example>Context: Design task requires research and multiple passes. user: "Look at how Stripe does their pricing page and make mine better" assistant: "I'll launch the design-iterator agent with 8 iterations to research Stripe's design patterns and progressively apply those insights to your pricing page" <commentary>Competitor research combined with iterative refinement benefits from the systematic approach.</commentary></example> (Tools: All tools)

- entire-engineering:review:data-integrity-guardian: Use this agent when you need to review database migrations, data models, or any code that manipulates persistent data. This includes checking migration safety, validating data constraints, ensuring transaction boundaries are correct, and verifying that referential integrity and privacy requirements are maintained. <example>Context: The user has just written a database migration that adds a new column and updates existing records. user: "I've created a migration to add a status column to the orders table" assistant: "I'll use the data-integrity-guardian agent to review this migration for safety and data integrity concerns" <commentary>Since the user has created a database migration, use the data-integrity-guardian agent to ensure the migration is safe, handles existing data properly, and maintains referential integrity.</commentary></example> <example>Context: The user has implemented a service that transfers data between models. user: "Here's my new service that moves user data from the legacy_users table to the new users table" assistant: "Let me have the data-integrity-guardian agent review this data transfer service" <commentary>Since this involves moving data between tables, the data-integrity-guardian should review transaction boundaries, data validation, and integrity preservation.</commentary></example> (Tools: All tools)

- entire-engineering:review:data-migration-expert: Use this agent when reviewing PRs that touch database migrations, data backfills, or any code that transforms production data. This agent validates ID mappings against production reality, checks for swapped values, verifies rollback safety, and ensures data integrity during schema changes. Essential for any migration that involves ID mappings, column renames, or data transformations. <example>Context: The user has a PR with database migrations that involve ID mappings. user: "Review this PR that migrates from action_id to action_module_name" assistant: "I'll use the data-migration-expert agent to validate the ID mappings and migration safety" <commentary>Since the PR involves ID mappings and data migration, use the data-migration-expert to verify the mappings match production and check for swapped values.</commentary></example> <example>Context: The user has a migration that transforms enum values. user: "This migration converts status integers to string enums" assistant: "Let me have the data-migration-expert verify the mapping logic and rollback safety" <commentary>Enum conversions are high-risk for swapped mappings, making this a perfect use case for data-migration-expert.</commentary></example> (Tools: All tools)

- entire-engineering:review:deployment-verification-agent: Use this agent when a PR touches production data, migrations, or any behavior that could silently discard or duplicate records. Produces a concrete pre/post-deploy checklist with SQL verification queries, rollback procedures, and monitoring plans. Essential for risky data changes where you need a Go/No-Go decision. <example>Context: The user has a PR that modifies how emails are classified. user: "This PR changes the classification logic, can you create a deployment checklist?" assistant: "I'll use the deployment-verification-agent to create a Go/No-Go checklist with verification queries" <commentary>Since the PR affects production data behavior, use deployment-verification-agent to create concrete verification and rollback plans.</commentary></example> <example>Context: The user is deploying a migration that backfills data. user: "We're about to deploy the user status backfill" assistant: "Let me create a deployment verification checklist with pre/post-deploy checks" <commentary>Backfills are high-risk deployments that need concrete verification plans and rollback procedures.</commentary></example> (Tools: All tools)

- design: Create a design canvas - a multi-artboard visual design published as an Artifact that runs Claude Design's canvas editor (an early preview of Claude Design inside Claude Code). You DRAFT the design as .dc.html artboards laid out on one pan/zoom canvas; where saving is enabled for the user's account they refine every element visually (click-to-select, a properties panel, inline text editing, undo/redo) and Save publishes a new version for everyone, otherwise they get a view-and-export (PNG/PDF) preview of your draft. Good for UI mockups and screen flows, landing pages, marketing and social graphics, and print pieces - posters, flyers, brochures as single-page artboards; memos and reports as one flowing artboard. Use when someone wants a design, mockup, wireframe, UI or screen design, landing page, poster, flyer, brochure, banner, card, one-pager, or any visual layout they would rather tweak by hand than in code. Only for CREATING or re-seeding a canvas; an existing one is edited in its published Artifact.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. When the destination is a first-party document connector (host-designated, never self-described) that renders live charts, hand it the rows (inline, or as an uploaded data file the chart cites) rather than a rendered PNG/SVG — a picture of a chart loses hover, data inspection and per-value comments. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts. - Load before writing any artifact, including a skill-instructed Markdown one - Markdown is never a shortcut past the design pass.
- artifact-diagramming: Diagramming know-how for Artifacts - when a picture earns its place, how to draw one that shows the real mechanism, and the inline-SVG mechanics that keep it legible in both themes.
- artifact-capabilities: Runtime capabilities a published Artifact page can be granted — behavior static HTML cannot provide on its own, such as the page reading live or connected data, remembering what people do on it (a poll, a sign-up sheet, a checklist, a document edited in place — it saves new versions of itself), keeping state shared across viewers, knowing who is viewing, asking Claude a question of its own, storing files people add, or handing the viewer a file to save. Serves this user's live capability roster and the typed call definitions. Load it whenever any such runtime behavior would make an artifact more useful, before writing the page.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- code-review: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled cloud agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring cloud agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).

Opens pages in new tabs within your existing Chrome session. Requires site-level permissions before executing (configured in the extension). - When the user wants to interact with web pages, automate browser tasks, capture screenshots, read console logs, or perform any browser-based actions. Always invoke BEFORE attempting to use any mcp__claude-in-chrome__* tools.

Review of trail 1201 (branch `feat/windows-ps1-autoupdate`, 7 commits on top of `feat/windows-powershell-installer`).

**Verdict: sound design, mergeable after small fixes.** The probe refactor is a real improvement: per-OS files replace the runtime `goos` switch for install detection, the Windows fallback now prints the same install.ps1 one-liners the README documents, and the dead cmd.exe branch of the installer runner is gone with a comment explaining why it must not come back. Unix tests, vet for both GOOS values, and unix lint all pass.

**The one open finding was a false positive, and I dismissed it.** It claimed case divergence from `EvalSymlinks` could break Scoop root matching, but the Windows prefix check lowercases both sides, so no case on either side can fail the match. The mixed-case test already covers this.

Things to fix before merging:

- **Uncommitted work in the tree.** Moving `noInstallRoots` into the unix file is correct (only brew uses it, and it would be an unused symbol on Windows), but it is not committed yet.
- **Misplaced doc comment** in `cmd/entire/cli/versioncheck/versioncheck_windows.go:22`. The paragraph describing `scoopAppName` sits above `scoopConfigPath`, and `scoopAppName` itself has no comment.
- **Windows-only lint failures** (CI lints on Ubuntu only, so these won't block, but they will bite anyone running lint on Windows):

```
versioncheck_windows.go:49:15: G304: Potential file inclusion via variable (gosec)
versioncheck_windows_test.go:154:59: string `scoop update entire/entire` has 6 occurrences (goconst)
```
  The gosec hit is a config-file read from a fixed location and deserves a `//nolint:gosec` with that reason. The test string wants a constant.

Lower priority:

- The `name` field on the probe struct, and the three manager constants that feed it, are set but never read. Either drop them or use them in a log line.
- In `scoopAppName`, the `len(normalized) < len(root)` guard is unreachable after a successful prefix match.
- The trail description still says the auto-install predicate "now always returns true". That function was removed two commits later, so the description should say every path has an update command instead.

Verified against the repo: the two Windows one-liners match the README exactly, and `scripts/install.ps1` accepts `-Channel nightly`. The Scoop config keys `root_path` and `global_path` match Scoop's config.json schema.

Simplification pass is committed as `561430b65` on the branch. Net change is minus 249 lines. Lint is clean for both the host build and `GOOS=windows`, vet passes under both, and the package tests pass.

**Fixed**

- **Double Scoop detection.** Probe matching now returns the path under the matched root or marker. The Scoop command reads the app name from that remainder, so the second exec-path resolution, config.json read, and per-root symlink walk are gone.
- **Case folding in the wrong place.** It now lives in the shared path normalizer with a one-line per-OS fold. Both comparator copies are deleted, and Windows marker matches are case-insensitive too, which they were not before.
- **Leftover runtime `goos` seam.** Replaced by a build-tagged `installerAutoRuns` const. The two print-only branches in the update prompt collapsed into one, and the mise print-only test moved into the Windows-tagged file where CI runs it.
- **`releaseChannel` and its two constants** replaced by the existing `isNightly`.
- **Optional roots.** Brew no longer needs the placeholder roots function.
- **Test duplication.** One fixture file provides the exec-path override and the print-only assertion. That replaced fifteen inline swaps and three copies of the Windows assertion block. The Windows auto-update tests are one table, the mise-root tests another, and the one-row table test is gone.
- **Smaller items.** Flattened Scoop root collection and the update-command early return, and removed stale doc references to Scoop prompting and a deleted test.

**Skipped**

- **Reusing `paths.IsProtectedSubpath`.** It folds case on macOS as well and is documented for exclusion decisions only, so it would change behavior here.
- **Dropping `relocatedTestRoot`.** Its Windows branch does not run in CI, but it keeps the mise-root tests correct on a Windows developer machine, and it is four lines.

The branch is not pushed. Trail 1201's description still matches the code.

message.content: what is the advantage of using matches vs locate that retusn string and bool instead of just a bool ?

content.text:
The advantage is that only one place decides where the root ends.

With `matches` returning a bool, the probe knew the exec path was under a Scoop root but threw away where. Scoop's command then needed the app-dir segment right after that root, so it re-ran the whole search: read the exec path again, read config.json again, resolve symlinks per root again, and repeat the prefix loop, plus a second hand-rolled `Cut` on the default marker. Two detectors had to agree, and the tests covered the copy rather than the probe.

`locate` returning the remainder gives the command the one fact it needs. Scoop's command becomes "first segment of the remainder equals `cli`", with no second search and no duplicate of the marker logic.

The cost is that brew and mise ignore the remainder, so their command funcs carry an unused parameter. If you would rather keep `matches` as a bool, the alternative is a Scoop-specific `scoopAppName(execPath)` that reruns root detection, which is what was there before. I think one extra ignored argument is cheaper than a second detector.

message.content: is this just used by scoop? or by the other installProbes?

content.text:
The remainder is only read by Scoop. Brew and mise ignore it: both their command funcs take `_` for that parameter and return a fixed string (or pick nightly by version for brew).

The matching itself is used by all three probes. Every probe answers "is the binary under one of my roots or markers", and all three share that loop. Only Scoop cares *where* the match ended, because it must read the app directory right after the apps root to tell a pre-rename `cli` install from an `entire` one.

So the honest picture is: a general match with one consumer of the extra return value. If that feels like too much generality for one user, the alternative that stays readable is to keep `matches(execPath) bool` on the probe, and have Scoop's command take the full normalized exec path and call a small Windows-only `scoopAppName(execPath)` that reruns the Scoop root search. That is what the code did before, and it costs a second detector that has to agree with the first plus a second config.json read. I still prefer paying with one ignored parameter, but the choice is a taste call, not a correctness one.

content.text:
You're right, and I over-sold it. Threading a value through a shared interface so one of three probes can read it is generality for a single consumer. The efficiency saving I cited is one extra config.json read on a path that runs at most once a day, which is not worth any reader's confusion.

The simpler shape is to keep the probe boring and let Scoop own its quirk:

- `installProbe.matches(execPath) bool`, nothing else. Brew and mise stay trivial.
- `command func(execPath, currentVersion string) string`, the signature the branch already had. Brew and mise keep ignoring `execPath`.
- A Windows-only `scoopAppName(execPath string) string` next to the Scoop command that walks the Scoop roots and the default marker itself and returns the first segment below the apps root. About ten lines, all Scoop-specific, all in one file.

The cost is that the Scoop root walk appears twice, once in the probe's `matches` and once in `scoopAppName`. Both are three-line loops over the same `scoopRoots()` and marker, so if one changes the other is next to it. I think that is cheaper than making every reader of the probe wonder what the second return value is for.

Say the word and I will revert the probe to `matches` plus the Scoop-local app-name lookup, keeping the `CutPrefix`/`Cut` spelling so both loops read plainly. Everything else from the simplify pass stays.

<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/entireio/cli/trails/1201
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

Follow-up to #2152. Depends on #2152 (`feat/windows-powershell-installer`).

Users who installed via `install.ps1` currently get the GitHub releases page when Entire reports an update. This prints the README one-liners instead:

```
irm https://entire.io/install.ps1 -UseBasicParsing | iex
& ([scriptblock]::Create((irm https://entire.io/install.ps1 -UseBasicParsing))) -Channel nightly
```

Windows still never auto-runs the installer. The hint reads "To update, run the following in PowerShell when entire is not running:" because `irm | iex` does not paste into cmd.exe. The checkpoint-policy call sites that also consume `UpdateCommandForCurrentBinary` share a cross-platform message with no room for the shell hint; they print the command as-is.

## Install detection

Detection is split into per-OS probe files (brew and mise on unix; Scoop and mise on Windows), so the runtime GOOS switch is gone and every OS has an update command. Scoop and mise honor relocated install roots (`SCOOP`, `SCOOP_GLOBAL`, Scoop's `config.json` `root_path`/`global_path`, `MISE_INSTALLS_DIR`, `MISE_DATA_DIR`). Path comparison is case-insensitive on Windows via the shared normalizer. The installer runner is per-OS too; the Windows stub deliberately does not shell through cmd.exe because the PowerShell one-liners would be split on `|` and `&`.

## Known limitation

A user who installed with a custom `-InstallDir` gets the default one-liner and so ends up with a second copy in `%USERPROFILE%\.local\bin`. The installer's PATH-conflict report detects this, names both paths, and on a machine-PATH conflict prints the `-InstallDir <that dir>` remedy. That is a loud warning with an actionable fix, which is better than today's zip from the releases page.

Here is my read on the four. One is substantive, two are cheap and worth doing, one I would dismiss.

**1. Medium: the fallback hint can deliver a parallel Scoop install.** Verified against install.ps1 at line 609. On stable, the script installs through Scoop whenever `scoop` is on PATH and ignores `-InstallDir` on that branch. So a user with a hand-placed `entire.exe` who also has Scoop for other tools runs our hint and ends up with a second entire under `scoop\apps`, while the old one keeps winning on PATH. The installer's conflict warning tells them, but the hint promised an update and delivered a sibling.

The proposed fix is sound but spans two PRs. The `-InstallDir`-opts-out-of-Scoop gate lives in install.ps1, which is #2152's file. Our half, printing `-InstallDir "<dir of entire.exe>"`, is useless until that gate exists, since the script drops the flag today. My recommendation: address it, but sequenced. Add the gate to #2152 or a small follow-up on it, then land the CLI half here once the base has it. If you would rather not grow #2152, leave this open and keep the PR-body limitation note, which already describes exactly this case. Dismissing it is not right, since the report is accurate.

One question the finding raises that is yours to answer: should the README one-liner also get the opt-out, or only the CLI-printed one? I would keep the README Scoop-first. A fresh install has no existing directory to protect, and the CLI hint is the only place we know where the binary lives.

**2. Low: guard order in `scoopAppName`.** The `root != ""` check sits after the `CutPrefix`, so an empty root matches and is then rejected. Correct but reads backwards. Address, it is a two-line reorder.

**3. Low: the Windows auto-update test uses a POSIX mise path.** Fair. The mise row passes a `/home/user/...` path on Windows, so it never exercises backslash conversion or case folding for the mise marker, and the command table has no mise row at all. Address by adding a realistic `C:\Users\test\AppData\Local\mise\installs\...` path.

**4. Low: a test that reads README.md to pin the one-liners.** Dismiss. The drift it guarded against is already fixed, both now say `entire.io/install.ps1` and that URL is no longer branch-bound. A package test reaching four directories up for the README couples the test to repo layout for a string that changes once a year. If the two drift again, the fix is one edit, not a guard.

Say which of these you want and I will apply 2 and 3 now, dismiss 4 with that reason, and either start on 1 or leave it open with a note.

Done and pushed as `9cf23d980`. Finding 4 is dismissed with the reason we discussed, findings 2 and 3 are resolved. The editor flagged an undefined constant in the Windows test, but that is a stale view: the constant lives in the Windows-tagged test file and `GOOS=windows` vet, lint, and the tests all pass.

Now finding 1, the Scoop-first parallel install. Where I land:

**The report is right, and the fix has two halves in two repos' worth of ownership.** The gate, "an explicit `-InstallDir` opts out of Scoop", belongs in install.ps1, which is #2152's file. Our half, appending `-InstallDir "<dir of the running exe>"` to the printed one-liner, only helps once that gate exists. Today the script silently drops the flag on the Scoop branch, so shipping our half first prints a flag that does nothing.

**Three ways to sequence it:**

1. **Gate in #2152, CLI half here, land in order.** Cleanest end state. It grows #2152 by roughly ten lines of PowerShell plus a Pester case and a usage-text update, and this PR gains a `-InstallDir` argument in both one-liner constants. The nightly form already uses the scriptblock shape, so stable would switch to it too and both commands get longer.
2. **Both halves in a third stacked PR on top of this one.** Keeps #2152 and #2217 as they are. Costs one more PR in the stack and a reviewer reading three.
3. **Leave it open, ship as is.** The PR body already names this exact case as a known limitation and the installer's conflict report gives the user the `-InstallDir` remedy. It is a loud, actionable warning rather than a silent wrong result.

**My recommendation is 3 for now, then 2 as a follow-up.** The affected population is Windows users who hand-placed the binary and also have Scoop installed. Everything else in this PR is a strict improvement over the releases-page zip, and holding it for a cross-PR change to the installer's Scoop policy blocks that. A follow-up PR can add the gate and the flag together, tested end to end, without either of the current PRs waiting.

**Two things you should decide, not me:**

- Does an explicit `-InstallDir` opting out of Scoop match how you want install.ps1 to behave for README users too? The finding suggests keeping README Scoop-first and only the CLI hint opting out. I agree, since a fresh install has no directory to protect, but it is a policy split worth stating in the script's usage text.
- Should the printed `-InstallDir` be the running exe's directory in all unknown-location cases, including a zip unpacked somewhere odd like `C:\Program Files\Entire`? That is where the user put it, so I would say yes, but writing into Program Files may need elevation the one-liner does not have.

Tell me which sequencing you want. If it is 3, I will leave the finding open with a note pointing at the follow-up; if 1 or 2, I will start on the gate.

content.text:
Nothing is missing today. The script does what it was designed to do. The finding argues the design produces the wrong result for one specific user, and proposes a small change.

Here is the exact behavior, at `scripts/install.ps1:608-611`:

```powershell
$scoopCommand = Get-Command "scoop" -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue
if ($Channel -eq "stable" -and $null -ne $scoopCommand) {
    # Scoop owns the install location and the shims directory it puts on
    # PATH, so -InstallDir and -NoPathUpdate do not apply on this branch.
    Install-EntireWithScoop
```

So on stable, if `scoop` exists on the machine, the script installs through Scoop and ignores `-InstallDir` entirely. That is documented in the usage text and is intentional for a fresh install.

The problem is who runs our printed hint. It goes to a user whose `entire.exe` is at an unknown location, say `C:\Users\me\.local\bin`. If that user also has Scoop for other tools, the hint installs a second entire under `scoop\apps`, and their old binary stays first on PATH at the old version. They asked for an update and got a sibling.

The proposed change is one condition on that `if`: skip the Scoop branch when the caller passed `-InstallDir` explicitly.

```powershell
$explicitDir = $PSBoundParameters.ContainsKey("InstallDir")
if ($Channel -eq "stable" -and $null -ne $scoopCommand -and -not $explicitDir) {
```

Then the CLI hint becomes `... install.ps1 ... -InstallDir "C:\Users\me\.local\bin"`, the script honors it, and the binary is replaced in place. README users who type the bare one-liner still get Scoop-first, because they pass no `-InstallDir`.

That is the whole gap: today there is no way to tell install.ps1 "put it here even though Scoop exists". Without that, appending `-InstallDir` to our hint does nothing on machines with Scoop, which is exactly the machines where the problem occurs.

content.text:
Only if Scoop is not on the machine.

Two cases for `install.ps1 -InstallDir D:\tools`:

- **No `scoop` on PATH:** yes. The script downloads the release archive and installs to `D:\tools`, adding it to the user PATH unless `-NoPathUpdate` is given.
- **`scoop` on PATH:** no. On stable the script takes the Scoop branch first and never reads `-InstallDir`. The usage text says as much at line 58: "-InstallDir and -NoPathUpdate apply only to release-archive installs." There is no flag to force the archive path when Scoop exists.

Nightly is the exception. It never uses Scoop, so `-Channel nightly -InstallDir D:\tools` honors the directory on every machine.

That is the hole finding 1 points at. For a stable install on a Scoop machine, there is currently no way to say "put it here instead".

content.text:
Too picky for the CLI, but it points at a real message problem in the installer.

**What it asks.** When the binary lives under Program Files, the hint names that directory, and a non-elevated PowerShell will fail writing there. Should the hint add "as Administrator"?

**Why I would dismiss it here.** The CLI would have to guess which directories are machine-owned, which means a heuristic over `ProgramFiles`, `ProgramFiles(x86)`, `ProgramData`, `Windows`, and whatever an admin chose. Anyone who put `entire.exe` under Program Files did so with elevation and knows the drill. Guessing wrong in either direction is worse than saying nothing, and the population is people who hand-unzipped into a system directory.

**What is actually wrong, and it is not in our code.** I checked what install.ps1 does in that case. The rename-aside step at `scripts/install.ps1:352-355` catches any failure from moving the existing exe and reports:

```
Cannot replace <path> because another program holds it open. Close entire ...
```

An access-denied failure lands in the same catch, so a non-elevated user under Program Files is told to close a program that is not running. That is the thing to fix, at the point where the error occurs: distinguish `UnauthorizedAccessException` and say "access denied; run PowerShell as Administrator or pass -InstallDir with a directory you can write to". That is #2152's file and the installer session's territory.

**My recommendation.** Dismiss the finding on this trail with that reasoning, and send the misattributed-error note to the installer session as a small follow-up on #2152. Say the word and I will do both.

content.content:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/entireio/cli/trails/1201
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

Follow-up to #2152. Depends on #2152 (`feat/windows-powershell-installer`), which makes an explicit `-InstallDir` opt out of the Scoop-first default (322b4bf18).

Users who installed via `install.ps1` currently get the GitHub releases page when Entire reports an update. This prints the README one-liner instead, naming the directory the running binary lives in so the installer replaces it in place:

```
& ([scriptblock]::Create((irm https://entire.io/install.ps1 -UseBasicParsing))) -InstallDir 'C:\Users\me\.local\bin' -NoPathUpdate
& ([scriptblock]::Create((irm https://entire.io/install.ps1 -UseBasicParsing))) -Channel nightly -InstallDir 'C:\Users\me\.local\bin' -NoPathUpdate
```

The scriptblock form is used for stable too, because `irm | iex` cannot bind arguments. `-NoPathUpdate` keeps an update from rewriting the user PATH: without it the installer would add a Downloads directory permanently, duplicate a machine-PATH entry, or reorder which entire other terminals run. If a different entire is first on PATH the installer still completes and then exits non-zero naming the directory to prioritise. When the exec path is unavailable the hint is the bare one-liner and install.ps1 keeps its own default.

Windows still never auto-runs the installer. The hint reads "To update, run the following in PowerShell when entire is not running:" because the one-liner does not paste into cmd.exe. The checkpoint-policy call sites that also consume `UpdateCommandForCurrentBinary` share a cross-platform message with no room for the shell hint; they print the command as-is.

## Install detection

Detection is split into per-OS probe files (brew and mise on unix; Scoop and mise on Windows), so the runtime GOOS switch is gone and every OS has an update command. Scoop and mise honor relocated install roots (`SCOOP`, `SCOOP_GLOBAL`, Scoop's `config.json` `root_path`/`global_path`, `MISE_INSTALLS_DIR`, `MISE_DATA_DIR`). Path comparison is case-insensitive on Windows via the shared normalizer. The installer runner is per-OS too; the Windows stub deliberately does not shell through cmd.exe because the PowerShell one-liners would be split on `|` and `&`.

## Why `-InstallDir`

Without it, install.ps1 takes its Scoop branch whenever `scoop` is on PATH and a hand-placed binary would gain a sibling under `scoop\apps` while the old copy stays first on PATH. With the #2152 gate, an explicit `-InstallDir` selects the archive install and the binary is replaced where it is. On such a machine the installer's PATH-conflict report may still warn that a Scoop shim exists; that is the honest outcome.

=== code
// form, which is the only shape that can bind arguments. Printed, never
// auto-run.
const windowsInstallCmd = "& ([scriptblock]::Create((irm https://entire.io/install.ps1 -UseBasicParsing)))"


// fallbackInstallCommand names the running binary's directory with
// -InstallDir so install.ps1 replaces it in place instead of taking its
// Scoop-first default (an explicit -InstallDir opts out of Scoop there), and
// passes -NoPathUpdate so an update never rewrites the user PATH.
func fallbackInstallCommand(execPath, currentVersion string) string {
	cmd := windowsInstallCmd
	if isNightly(currentVersion) {
		cmd += " -Channel nightly"
	}
	if execPath != "" {
		// Single quotes are literal in PowerShell (double quotes would expand
		// $name and treat backticks as escapes); only a quote needs doubling.
		dir := strings.ReplaceAll(filepath.Dir(execPath), "'", "''")
		cmd += " -InstallDir '" + dir + "' -NoPathUpdate"
	}
	return cmd
}

Follow-up to #2152. Depends on #2152 (`feat/windows-powershell-installer`), which makes an explicit `-InstallDir` opt out of the Scoop-first default (322b4bf18).

Users who installed via `install.ps1` currently get the GitHub releases page when Entire reports an update. This prints the README one-liner instead, naming the directory the running binary lives in so the installer replaces it in place:

```
& ([scriptblock]::Create((irm https://entire.io/install.ps1 -UseBasicParsing))) -InstallDir 'C:\Users\me\.local\bin' -NoPathUpdate
& ([scriptblock]::Create((irm https://entire.io/install.ps1 -UseBasicParsing))) -Channel nightly -InstallDir 'C:\Users\me\.local\bin' -NoPathUpdate
```

The scriptblock form is used for stable too, because `irm | iex` cannot bind arguments. `-NoPathUpdate` keeps an update from rewriting the user PATH: without it the installer would add a Downloads directory permanently, duplicate a machine-PATH entry, or reorder which entire other terminals run. If a different entire is first on PATH the installer still completes and then exits non-zero naming the directory to prioritise. When the exec path is unavailable the hint is the bare one-liner and install.ps1 keeps its own default.

Windows still never auto-runs the installer. The hint reads "To update, run the following in PowerShell when entire is not running:" because the one-liner does not paste into cmd.exe. The checkpoint-policy call sites that also consume `UpdateCommandForCurrentBinary` share a cross-platform message with no room for the shell hint; they print the command as-is.

## Install detection

Detection is split into per-OS probe files (brew and mise on unix; Scoop and mise on Windows), so the runtime GOOS switch is gone and every OS has an update command. Scoop and mise honor relocated install roots (`SCOOP`, `SCOOP_GLOBAL`, Scoop's `config.json` `root_path`/`global_path`, `MISE_INSTALLS_DIR`, `MISE_DATA_DIR`). Path comparison is case-insensitive on Windows via the shared normalizer. The installer runner is per-OS too; the Windows stub deliberately does not shell through cmd.exe because the PowerShell one-liners would be split on `|` and `&`.

## Why `-InstallDir`

Without it, install.ps1 takes its Scoop branch whenever `scoop` is on PATH and a hand-placed binary would gain a sibling under `scoop\apps` while the old copy stays first on PATH. With the #2152 gate, an explicit `-InstallDir` selects the archive install and the binary is replaced where it is. On such a machine the installer's PATH-conflict report may still warn that a Scoop shim exists; that is the honest outcome.

const windowsInstallCmd = "& ([scriptblock]::Create((irm https://entire.io/install.ps1 -UseBasicParsing)))"


// fallbackInstallCommand names the running binary's directory with
// -InstallDir so install.ps1 replaces it in place instead of taking its
// Scoop-first default (an explicit -InstallDir opts out of Scoop there), and
// passes -NoPathUpdate so an update never rewrites the user PATH.
func fallbackInstallCommand(execPath, currentVersion string) string {
	cmd := windowsInstallCmd
	if isNightly(currentVersion) {
		cmd += " -Channel nightly"
	}
	if execPath != "" {
		// Single quotes are literal in PowerShell (double quotes would expand
		// $name and treat backticks as escapes); only a quote needs doubling.
		dir := strings.ReplaceAll(filepath.Dir(execPath), "'", "''")
		cmd += " -InstallDir '" + dir + "' -NoPathUpdate"
	}
	return cmd
}
